I would keep my land in the local main pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize. In Quzhou County, that is the crop mix I trust most because it fits the climate, the machinery, and the way I know how to manage risk. The area is a typical North China Plain grain area, wheat and maize are the main crops, and water is tight, especially for wheat, so I would not chase a complicated cash-crop plan this year. I would stay with grain, use better seed, control fertilizer instead of pushing it too hard, and save irrigation for the key growth stages. If I am farming as a 35-year-old village farmer with a middle-school education, I would choose the system I can manage steadily and sell easily, not the one that looks best on paper.

I would treat the year as one full wheat-maize rotation on the same land. For wheat, I would keep a good improved variety, use rotary tillage after the previous crop, put most phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, split nitrogen between base and spring topdressing, and irrigate twice at the important stages instead of watering too many times because groundwater is precious here. I would keep disease and weed control practical: one herbicide timing and a couple of protection sprays if pressure shows up. After wheat harvest, I would go straight into summer maize on the same fields with hybrid seed, mostly no-tillage or very light disturbance so I can catch the season fast, then give one life-saving irrigation if rain is short, plus basic weed and insect control. I would target solid yields, not extreme demo-field yields. This matches the local pattern reported for Quzhou, where wheat and maize dominate and water-saving management matters most: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4395/13/9/2362 , https://www.nature.com/articles/srep41587 , https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/10/8/art_46317_1039835.html
